sections.heading: Finding my joy in you even when praise feels weak
sections.text:
God, you are my deepest joy. When I praise you, my heart is lifted because you are not cold or empty—you are the source of real delight, and you bless the person who is glad in you.

But I know my heart is not as steady as it should be. There is still resistance in me, and I do not always praise you with the freedom, warmth, and honesty you deserve. Even so, I want to keep resting in who you are: your beauty, your goodness, your mercy, and your faithful love. In Jesus, you are more wonderful than I can put into words, and I want the thought of you to become my true pleasure.
theological_themes: God himself is the believer’s joy, not merely the giver of joys.
Praise is both a duty and a gift that lifts the heart toward God.
Even weak praise can rest in God’s unchanging goodness and mercy revealed in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm names God as the worshiper’s exceeding joy and connects that joy directly with praise. It grounds the prayer’s movement from delight in God to singing and worship.
David locates fullness of joy in God’s presence, not in changing circumstances. That supports the prayer’s claim that God himself is a fountain of delight.

sections.heading: Being honest about the rebellion still in me
sections.text:
Lord, I have to admit that I am not only weak; sometimes I still resist you. You have given me new life, but there are corrupt desires in me that still pull away from you and push back against your rule. My old nature wanders, argues, and looks for ways to live without you.

Please do not let me excuse that. Teach me to see it clearly and bring it into the light before you.
theological_themes: Regeneration does not remove the believer’s ongoing conflict with sin in this life.
Honest confession refuses to excuse inward resistance to God.
The Christian life involves warfare between the flesh and the Spirit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the ongoing conflict between the desires of the flesh and the Spirit in believers. This helps express how a renewed person can still experience real inward opposition to God.

John warns believers against denying remaining sin and calls them to honest confession. The prayer’s frank admission of corruption belongs within that biblical pattern of coming into the light before God.

sections.heading: Asking you to search what is real in me
sections.text:
Help me praise you with a heart that is truly yielded to you. Make me willing to examine myself carefully, not in panic or pride, but honestly before your face.

Let me ask the hard questions: Have I truly been born again? Do I bear the family likeness of your children? Are my sorrows the kind that come from repentance, not just from being exposed or disappointed? Are my joys the joys of faith, not just religious feeling? Is my confidence in Christ producing love and making me cleaner inside?

Please make what is real stronger, and expose what is false before it hardens.
theological_themes: Self-examination is a biblical practice when done before God and in dependence on grace.
True faith bears fruit in love, repentance, holiness, and the witness of the Spirit.
Godly grief differs from mere regret because it turns the heart back to God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls the church to examine whether they are in the faith, which supports the prayer’s serious questions about spiritual reality rather than mere appearance.

Paul teaches that God’s children are led by the Spirit and receive the Spirit’s witness of adoption. This speaks directly to the prayer’s concern that the worshiper’s spirit be the spirit of God’s children.
Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief. This helps clarify the prayer’s request for sorrows that belong to a repentant heart.
Paul says what counts in Christ is faith working through love. That grounds the prayer’s concern that confidence in Christ should show itself in love and purification.

sections.heading: Letting faith show up in private and in public
sections.text:
Give me the quiet fruit of faith where no one sees me, in my thoughts, motives, habits, and hidden choices. And give me the public fruit of faith too, in the way I speak, lead, serve, and live before others.

Do not let my ministry outrun my soul. Make my life, both unseen and seen, agree with the gospel I proclaim.
theological_themes: Faith is meant to bear visible fruit in character and conduct.
Private holiness and public ministry must not be separated.
Those who serve others spiritually must watch both their teaching and their life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells Timothy to keep close watch on himself and on his teaching, showing that public ministry and personal holiness belong together. This fits the prayer’s request for faith’s results in both secret character and public life.
James teaches that faith without works is dead, not because works replace faith, but because living faith bears fruit. This supports the prayer’s desire for faith to become visible in real obedience.

sections.heading: Hold my heart by the love of Christ
sections.text:
Wrap my heart in the cords of your love, and hold me so tightly that I do not slip away. Let the wounds of my Savior move me more deeply than the power, pressure, or approval of important people.

Give me a love for you that becomes larger than every rival love. Keep me faithful to Christ, my beloved, so that I do not betray the union you have given me with him.
theological_themes: God’s love holds and constrains the believer.
Christ’s wounds and sacrificial death are the deepest motive for obedience.
Union with Christ calls for spiritual faithfulness and undivided love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says the love of Christ controls believers because Christ died for them, so they no longer live for themselves. This directly supports the prayer’s desire to be governed more by Christ’s wounds than by worldly power.
Jesus promises that his sheep are held securely in his hand and the Father’s hand. This gives biblical grounding to the plea that God would hold the worshiper and never let him go.
Paul portrays Christ as the bridegroom who loves and purifies his people. This illuminates the prayer’s language of faithful union with the beloved without reducing it to mere emotion.

sections.heading: Clean out what still does not belong to you
sections.text:
There is still so much in me that has not been brought under your rule. There are rooms in my heart where selfish desires still trade and bargain as if they own the place.

Come and drive out what does not belong in your temple. Clear away the greed, pride, impurity, and divided desires that still live in me. In their place, give me clean desires, holy longings, and a deeper hunger to be completely yours.
theological_themes: The believer belongs to God and is called to holiness in body and spirit.
Remaining sin must be actively put away, not politely managed.
Sanctification includes both cleansing from sin and the formation of new holy desires.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God because it was bought with a price. This supports the prayer’s temple imagery and its plea that what dishonors God be removed.

Paul urges believers, in light of God’s promises, to cleanse themselves from defilement and pursue holiness. This fits the request for corrupt desires to be displaced by longings for perfect holiness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s searching self-examination, including the question of whether the speaker is truly born again, may feel unsettling to traditions that emphasize assurance more strongly. I preserved the Puritan concern while framing it as honest examination before God rather than anxious introspection detached from grace.

The phrase about not violating a “chaste union with the beloved” uses bridal and purity imagery for the believer’s relationship to Christ. I rendered it as faithfulness to union with Christ to preserve the theological meaning without importing unnecessarily archaic or romanticized language.
significant_interpretive_choices: “The Saviour’s wounds” was interpreted as Christ’s crucifixion and atoning love functioning as the chief motive for obedience, stronger than social power or human authority represented by “the sceptre of princes.”

“Buyers and sellers of my soul’s temple” was treated as an inward application of the temple-cleansing image: selfish, corrupt desires occupying what belongs to God. I connected it with the believer as the Spirit’s temple rather than implying that John 2 directly teaches an allegory of the soul.

“Give me the sweet results of faith, in my secret character, and in my public life” was rendered with explicit reference to ministry because the prayer’s title and collection section identify the speaker as a minister, while still keeping the language broad enough for personal prayer.
